proposal: The Mandate states that federal education policy should be limited and the Department should ultimately be eliminated. It calls on the next administration to work with Congress on a Department of Education Reorganization Act (or liquidating authority act) that reforms, eliminates, or moves the Department's programs and offices, and it recommends a report to Congress on consolidating the Department and trimming nonessential staff.
remaining: Congress enacts a statute (a Reorganization Act or equivalent) that repeals the Department of Education Organization Act or directs the transfer of statutory functions; none has passed.
Under the interagency agreements ED keeps statutory responsibility for the programs; remaining functions (for example data and research) have not all been assigned.

status_summary: As of 2026-10-07 the Department has not been abolished by statute and still operates. Executive Order 14242 (2025-03-20) directs the Secretary to facilitate closure to the extent permitted by law. A March 2025 reduction in force, plus retirements and separation incentives, cut the workforce by about half according to Federal News Network, and the Supreme Court stayed the lower-court injunction against the layoffs on 2025-07-14. The Department has since signed interagency agreements moving program administration to other agencies, most recently four agreements announced on 2026-06-16 covering special education and civil rights functions (see c11-02, c11-03, c11-04, c11-07). Congress funded the Department at about $79 billion for FY2026 and did not adopt the requested cut. In July 2026 a House committee advanced bills to codify the transfers while a Senate committee advanced a bill to block some of them.

timeline.event: ED carries out a reduction in force of 1,378 employees, announced 2025-03-11.

Executive Order 14242 signed. It directs the Secretary to facilitate closure of the Department to the maximum extent appropriate and permitted by law and to return authority to states, and it states that implementation is subject to law and appropriations.
timeline.source: American Presidency Project (text of the order)

timeline.event: Judge Myong Joun (D. Mass.) issues a preliminary injunction in New York v. McMahon that would have blocked the March reduction in force, required reinstatement, and barred moving the loan portfolio and special education programs.
Supreme Court grants the government's application and stays the May 22 injunction pending appeal and any certiorari petition. Justices Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson dissent.

Plaintiffs in the consolidated Somerville v. Trump and New York v. McMahon cases file an amended complaint challenging the transfer of programs to other agencies; a second amended complaint followed on 2026-01-09 per a Hobbs Straus memo.

Congress passes FY2026 Education Department appropriations (exact day not given in sources; February 2026). Federal News Network reports about $79 billion in discretionary funding and rejection of a requested $12 billion cut and of proposed program moves. The statute does not bar interagency agreements; a nonbinding explanatory statement discourages moving core responsibilities.

ED announces four new interagency agreements, added to ten previously announced: special education programs and Rehabilitation Services Administration programs to HHS (Administration on Disabilities); the Office for Civil Rights, student privacy enforcement and four equity assistance centers to Justice. ED says it keeps enforcing special education law and OCR decides whether to pursue administrative enforcement.

Senate HELP Committee advances S. 5046, 13-9, which would bar transferring four ED offices (special education, elementary and secondary, postsecondary, Indian education) through interagency agreements. A House committee had earlier voted along party lines to codify many of the transfers (see c11-02).

A Senate press release from Sen. Warren states that the ED Office of Inspector General agreed to open an investigation of ED's management of its interagency agreement with the Department of Labor for higher education programs.
